claims.text: High configurational entropy stabilizes near-equiatomic multimetal alloys as simple solid solutions rather than intermetallic or segregated phases.
Lattice distortion arising from differences among constituent atoms lowers atomic diffusivity in high-entropy alloys.
Complex interactions among multiple elements govern lattice distortion and atomic diffusion rates.
High configurational entropy itself creates a rugged energy landscape that raises activation barriers for atomic diffusion.
Suppressed atomic mobility counteracts thermally driven diffusion that would otherwise cause phase segregation and chemical instability.

Quinary-or-higher nanoparticles will retain a single-phase solid solution with minimal segregation or secondary-phase formation throughout a 473–1923 K ramp under catalytic or thermoelectric operating conditions.
Formation of homogeneous five-metal nanoparticles without segregation is possible after brief heating to 2000–2300 K followed by rapid cooling.
The high-temperature synthesis result supports long-term structural and chemical stability during a gradual 473–1923 K operating ramp.
Lower-component binary or ternary nanoparticles will show phase separation earlier than the high-entropy nanoparticles under identical conditions.
Lower-component nanoparticles will exhibit more rapid atomic diffusion than the high-entropy nanoparticles.
Binary and ternary nanoparticle systems historically display increased diffusion and phase segregation at high temperatures.
The stability prediction depends on the nanoparticles being equiatomic and initially homogeneous single-phase solid solutions.

A five-component CoCrFeMnNi alloy can be kinetically constrained in a metastable fcc polymorph, while its high-temperature fcc phase is stable relative to hcp under the reported pressure-heating conditions.
The exact transformation temperatures and quantitative diffusion-rate differences between high-entropy and lower-component nanoparticles are uncertain.

Comparable or greater diffusion, segregation, or secondary-phase formation in the high-entropy nanoparticles relative to the lower-component controls would falsify the proposed intrinsic mobility suppression.
